metadata.purpose: Take apart the Build MCP Server skill: explain the three deployment paths and what each optimizes for, evaluate the two tool-design patterns against action-space size, and name the cost of a vague tool description. Land the carry-out that the skill asks four questions — deployment, users, action count, auth — before any code exists, and skipping that order costs a rewrite, not a tweak.

beats.narration_text: Take the deployment matrix apart. Three paths, ranked. Remote HTTP is the default because it optimizes for the thing that actually kills MCP servers in practice — install friction. One server, zero installs on the user's machine, and OAuth flows work the way OAuth is supposed to work, with real redirect handling. The trade-off it accepts: your server can't touch the user's local files. MCPB — Model Context Protocol Bundle — is the sanctioned local packaging format: server plus runtime, shipped as one artifact. Reach for it when the server has to read local files, drive a desktop app, or talk to something on localhost. Local stdio via npx or uvx works for a personal prototype and falls apart the moment you try to distribute it — no clean install story, no update story — so treat it as a stepping stone and flag the MCPB upgrade path on the handoff. The decision matrix covers seven scenarios: small SaaS API goes remote, large SaaS goes remote with search-plus-execute, UI widgets go MCP app, local desktop goes MCPB. Pick the path first and the rest of the design writes against a target instead of into open air.

production_viz.label: THREE DEPLOYMENT PATHS
production_viz.caption: remote HTTP default · unless local machine required

beats.narration_text: Tool design has two patterns, chosen by size. Pattern A: one tool per action. Works when the action space is under about fifteen operations. Give each one a dedicated tool with a tight description and schema; Claude reads the list once at registration and knows exactly what's on the menu. Pattern B: search-plus-execute. When you're wrapping a large API — dozens to hundreds of endpoints — listing every operation floods Claude's context window and degrades model performance for everything else the session is trying to do. The fix is two tools instead of hundreds: search-actions returns the operations matching a natural-language intent, and execute-action runs one by ID. Context stays lean; the long tail lives in the search index, not the tool list. The hybrid promotes the three to five most-used actions to dedicated tools and keeps the rest behind search. Beyond tools, three more primitives exist and most builds don't use them. Resources — host-browsable docs and data the client can page through. Prompts — user-triggered slash commands. Elicitation — a spec-native way to ask the user something mid-tool without building your own UI. Most servers only need tools. Knowing the other three exists is what stops you from reinventing them badly.

production_viz.label: TWO TOOL-DESIGN PATTERNS
production_viz.caption: large surface: search-plus-execute keeps context lean

beats.narration_text: Here's a subtlety in how well any of this works once the server actually ships. Claude picks a tool by reading its description, not its name. That sounds obvious and it isn't — a description that just restates the tool's name, 'creates an issue' for create-issue, gives Claude nothing to decide with when a sibling tool like update-issue is sitting right next to it. The name is a label. The description is the trigger clause. The more specific it is — when this fires, on what shape of request, in what context — the more reliably Claude reaches for the right tool at the right moment. Vague description, wrong dispatch, no stack trace to tell you which one lost.

production_viz.label: THE DESCRIPTION DECIDES
production_viz.caption: a vague description blurs similar tools together

beats.narration_text: Build MCP Server asks four questions — deployment, users, action count, auth — before a line of code exists. Skip that order and you don't get to tweak the server later. You rewrite it.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I want to design an MCP server that wraps the GitHub API, and I want to make the four decisions up front instead of scaffolding blind. One — deployment: pick between remote HTTP, MCPB, and stdio, decide which one fits GitHub API access, and explain the trade-off you're taking. Two — users: state whether this is single-user or multi-tenant, and what that changes about auth. Three — action count: list the operations you actually need — create issues, search repositories, get pull request details at minimum — and decide whether to expose them as one-tool-per-action or search-plus-execute, given the size of the GitHub API. Four — auth: choose a strategy, personal access token or OAuth, and justify it against the deployment choice. Then draft the tool definitions with descriptions that state when Claude should reach for each one — not what the tool is called. Critique your own descriptions: which is the vaguest, and how would you tighten it so Claude picks it over its siblings? Go deeper: ask the same model to work out where the search-plus-execute cutover actually sits for the GitHub API — count the endpoints you'd realistically want exposed, and design a hybrid where the three to five most-called operations get dedicated tools while the rest live behind search-actions and execute-action. Then have it name what breaks when a promoted tool changes shape, and how you'd notice.
